 and the outer cylinder is grounded. The annular region between the cylinders is filled with a material of dielectric constant 
. Consider an imaginary plane of the same length 
 at a distance 
 from the common axis of the cylinders. This plane is parallel to the axis of the cylinders. The cross-sectional view of this arrangement is shown in Fig. 2. Ignoring edge effects, the flux of the electric field through the plane is (

Given: Inner-cylinder radius: a, Outer-cylinder radius: b, with 0<a<b, Cylinder length: L, Charge on the inner cylinder: Q, Relative dielectric constant of the annular medium: K, Permittivity of the annular medium: K\varepsilon_0, Distance of the longitudinal plane from the common axis: d\ge 0, The plane is parallel to the common cylinder axis and has length L, The dielectric annulus occupies a\le \rho\le b, Edge effects are neglected
Find: The electric flux \Phi through the portion of the longitudinal plane lying in the dielectric annulus, including its dependence on d.

1. Set up the coaxial geometry and coordinate system
   ρ=√(x²+y²), x=d, ρ=√(d²+y²)
   Take the common cylinder axis as the z-axis. In a cross-section perpendicular to that axis, the longitudinal plane appears as the line x=d. A point on this plane has coordinates (d,y), so its radial distance from the axis is \rho=\sqrt{d^2+y^2}. The plane normal is chosen in the +x direction; reversing the normal reverses the final sign.

2. Use Gauss's law to determine the radial electric field
   E(ρ)(2πρ L)=(Q)/(Kvarepsilon ₀)
   Choose a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius \rho and length L, with a\le\rho\le b. The electric field is radial and has constant magnitude on the curved Gaussian surface. There is no flux through the end caps because the field is perpendicular to the cylinder axis. Applying Gauss's law gives the displayed relation.

3. Rearrange Gauss's-law result for the field magnitude
   E(ρ)=(Q)/(2π Kvarepsilon ₀Lρ)
   Divide the Gauss-law equation by 2\pi\rho L. The field points radially outward for Q>0 and radially inward for Q<0. The magnitude used in the flux integral is therefore E(\rho)=Q/(2\pi K\varepsilon_0L\rho) when Q denotes the signed charge with the chosen outward radial direction.

4. Write the normal component of the field on the plane
   mathbf E·mathbf n=E(ρ)(d)/(ρ)=(Qd)/(2π Kvarepsilon ₀L(d²+y²))
   On x=d, the radial unit vector has x-component d/\rho. Since the plane normal is \hat{\mathbf n}=\hat{\mathbf x}, the normal component is E_x=E(\rho)d/\rho. Substituting \rho=\sqrt{d^2+y^2} into the field expression gives the final form.

5. Express the differential area and flux integral
   dA=dy dz, Φ=∫ ∫ mathbf E·mathbf n dy dz
   The longitudinal plane is spanned by the y- and z-directions, so an area element is dy\,dz. The field is independent of z, and the plane extends through the full cylinder length L. Therefore the z-integration supplies a factor L, which will cancel the L in the field magnitude.

6. Determine where the longitudinal plane intersects the annulus
   ale √(d²+y²)le b
   The plane contributes only where its points satisfy the annular condition a\le\rho\le b. Squaring gives the radial bounds in y. These bounds change depending on whether the line x=d lies inside the inner cylinder, inside the annulus, or outside the outer cylinder.

7. Case I: plane lies inside the inner cylinder, d<a
   √(a²-d²)le |y|le √(b²-d²)
   When d<a, the line x=d passes through the inner conducting cylinder near y=0. The dielectric occurs in two symmetric strips: one at positive y and one at negative y. Thus the flux integral is twice the integral over the positive-y strip.

8. Evaluate the flux for d<a
   begin alignedΦ&=2L∫√₍ₐ^₂₋d^₂₎√⁽ᵇ^²⁻ᵈ^²⁾(Qd)/(2π Kvarepsilon ₀L(d²+y²)) dy\\[2pt]&=(Q)/(π Kvarepsilon ₀) [cos ⁻¹ ((d)/(b) )-cos ⁻¹ ((d)/(a) ) ]end aligned
   The factor 2 accounts for the positive- and negative-y strips. The factor L from the area integration cancels the L in E. Using \int d\,dy/(d^2+y^2)=\tan^{-1}(y/d) for d>0, together with \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{r^2-d^2}/d)=\cos^{-1}(d/r) on the stated branch, produces the displayed result. At d=0, the result is understood by continuity and gives zero flux.

9. Case II: plane lies in the annular region, a\le d<b
   -√(b²-d²)le yle √(b²-d²)
   When a\le d<b, every point on the line x=d has \rho\ge d\ge a, so the line does not enter the inner conductor. The entire chord inside the outer cylinder lies in the dielectric annulus.

10. Evaluate the flux for a\le d<b
   begin alignedΦ&=L∫₋√₍b^₂₋d^₂₎√⁽ᵇ^²⁻ᵈ^²⁾(Qd)/(2π Kvarepsilon ₀L(d²+y²)) dy\\[2pt]&=(Q)/(π Kvarepsilon ₀)cos ⁻¹ ((d)/(b) )
end aligned
   The interval is symmetric, so the integral can equivalently be written as twice the integral from 0 to \sqrt{b^2-d^2}. After cancellation of L and evaluation of the elementary integral, the flux depends only on the outer-cylinder chord angle. At d=a this agrees continuously with the result from Case I.

11. Case III: plane lies outside the outer cylinder, d\ge b
   Φ=0
   If d\ge b, the line x=d has radial distance \rho\ge d\ge b at every point. It therefore does not intersect the dielectric annulus, so there is no contributing surface area and the flux is zero.

12. Combine the three geometric cases
   boxed Φ(d)=begin cases (Q)/(π Kvarepsilon ₀) [cos ⁻¹ ((d)/(b) )-cos ⁻¹ ((d)/(a) ) ],&0le d<a,\\[10pt] (Q)/(π Kvarepsilon ₀)cos ⁻¹ ((d)/(b) ),&ale d<b,\\[10pt]0,&dge b.end cases
   The first expression applies when the plane cuts through the inner-cylinder exclusion region, the second when the plane lies within the annular cross-section, and the third when the plane misses the capacitor entirely. For the opposite plane normal, multiply the complete piecewise result by -1. The cylinder length L cancels, so the final flux is independent of L under the long-cylinder approximation.

Answer: boxed Φ(d)=begin cases (Q)/(π Kvarepsilon ₀) [cos ⁻¹ ((d)/(b) )-cos ⁻¹ ((d)/(a) ) ],&0le d<a,\\[10pt] (Q)/(π Kvarepsilon ₀)cos ⁻¹ ((d)/(b) ),&ale d<b,\\[10pt]0,&dge b,end cases
For a coaxial capacitor with inner radius a, outer radius b, length L, charge Q, and dielectric permittivity K\varepsilon_0, Gauss's law gives E(\rho)=Q/(2\pi K\varepsilon_0L\rho). On the longitudinal plane x=d, the normal component is E_n=Qd/[2\pi K\varepsilon_0L(d^2+y^2)]. Integrating E_n over only the portion satisfying a\le\sqrt{d^2+y^2}\le b gives the boxed piecewise result. The length L cancels. The sign shown corresponds to a normal directed toward increasing x; reversing the normal reverses the sign.

12 steps, 12 slides — 5 step(s) sympy could not prove — 8% of slides draw a figure

operations.title: Coaxial geometry
operations.caption: \rho=\sqrt{x^2+y^2},\qquad x=d,\qquad \rho=\sqrt{d^2+y^2}
operations.narration: Take the common cylinder axis along z. In the perpendicular cross-section, the longitudinal plane becomes the line x equals d, and a point on it has radial distance rho equal to the square root of d squared plus y squared.

operations.title: Gaussian cylinder
operations.caption: E(\rho)(2\pi\rho L)=\frac{Q}{K\varepsilon_0}
operations.narration: Use a coaxial Gaussian cylinder of radius rho and length L, with rho between a and b. Only its curved surface contributes because the radial field has no flux through the end caps.

operations.title: Radial field
operations.caption: E(\rho)=\frac{Q}{2\pi K\varepsilon_0L\rho}
operations.narration: Dividing by the curved Gaussian area gives the field magnitude. For positive Q it points radially outward; for negative Q the direction reverses.

operations.title: Normal component
operations.caption: \mathbf E\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\frac{Qd}{2\pi K\varepsilon_0L(d^2+y^2)}
operations.narration: At the point d comma y, the radial unit vector has x-component d over rho. Projecting the radial field onto the positive x normal gives the displayed normal component.

operations.title: Surface element
operations.caption: dA=dy\,dz,\qquad \Phi=\int\!\!\int \mathbf E\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dy\,dz
operations.narration: The plane is spanned by y and z, so its area element is dy dz. Integrating through the full length supplies a factor L, which will cancel the L in the field expression.

operations.title: Where flux exists
operations.caption: a\le\sqrt{d^2+y^2}\le b
operations.narration: The plane contributes only where its points lie in the dielectric annulus. This radial condition determines the allowed y-interval, which changes as d crosses a and b.

operations.title: Case I: d below a
operations.caption: \sqrt{a^2-d^2}\le |y|\le\sqrt{b^2-d^2}
operations.narration: When d is less than a, the line passes through the inner conducting region near y equals zero. The dielectric therefore appears in two symmetric strips.

operations.title: Evaluate Case I
operations.caption: \Phi=\frac{Q}{\pi K\varepsilon_0}\left[\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{d}{b}\right)-\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{d}{a}\right)\right]
operations.narration: The two strips give twice the positive-y integral. Substitution and cancellation of L produce the difference of two inverse-cosine terms; at d equals zero, the result is zero by continuity.

operations.title: Case II: inside annulus
operations.caption: -\sqrt{b^2-d^2}\le y\le\sqrt{b^2-d^2}
operations.narration: For d between a and b, every point on the line has rho at least d, so it is already outside the inner conductor. The complete chord inside the outer cylinder lies in the dielectric.

operations.title: Evaluate Case II
operations.caption: \Phi=\frac{Q}{\pi K\varepsilon_0}\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{d}{b}\right)
operations.narration: Integrating across the entire symmetric chord again cancels L. Only the outer-cylinder endpoint angle remains, and this agrees continuously with Case I at d equals a.

operations.title: Case III: outside
operations.caption: \Phi=0
operations.narration: If d is at least b, the line lies entirely outside the outer cylinder. It does not intersect the dielectric annulus, so the flux is zero.

operations.title: Final answer
operations.caption: \boxed{\Phi(d)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle \frac{Q}{\pi K\varepsilon_0}\left[\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{d}{b}\right)-\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{d}{a}\right)\right],&0\le d<a,\\[6pt]\displaystyle \frac{Q}{\pi K\varepsilon_0}\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{d}{b}\right),&a\le d<b,\\[6pt]0,&d\ge b.\end{cases}}
operations.narration: The flux is determined by which part of the annulus the longitudinal plane cuts. The cylinder length L cancels, and reversing the chosen normal reverses the sign of the complete result.
